newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda appeals to United Nations for legal aid.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda appeals to United Nations for legal aid.

text.p: Rwanda has appealed to the United Nations for funds to facilitate legal aid for more than 90,000 genocide suspects held across the tiny central African nation, a minister said on Saturday.
Deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima told Reuters: "Our ministry has requested funding to provide defence lawyers for genocide suspects."
He added: "This funding has been requested from the U.N. Development Programme (UNDP)."
Gahima declined to disclose how much was being sought to fund the trials, conducted parallel to ones at the U.N. Rwanda war crimes tribunal in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
The Rwandan government is privately dismissive of the U.N. court as an inept and wasteful exercise and has embarked on its own prosecutions against the detained Hutu suspects.
The U.N. court, which had a budget of $36 million in 1996, has indicted 21 suspects of whom 13 are in custody.
The cash appeal came over a week after Rwanda tried and sentenced to death two genocide suspects in a trial highly criticised because the accused had no defence lawyers.
The two, who have 15 days in which to appeal against the sentence, were found guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity. They face a firing squad if their appeals are unsuccessful.
Rwanda has scheduled more trials for next week.

Froduald Karamira, the most prominent of those detained by Rwanda, will go on trial next Tuesday in the Rwandan capital Kigali. Karamira was arrested at Addis Ababa airport in June last year and extradited to Rwanda.
International human rights groups, while welcoming the trials, have deplored serious irregularities accompanying the process such as lack of defence lawyers for the accused.

On Thursday, the U.N. tribunal in Tanzania reopened the trial of a Hutu former government official, Jean-Paul Akayesu, accused of ordering the slaughter of Tutsis and moderate Hutus during the 1994 genoicde.

Akayesu is a former mayor in central Rwanda's Taba commune and has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The prosecution says the crimes were committed between April and June 1994 when an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
The first witness to appear before the court, a Tutsi woman, testified against Akayesu who faces life imprisonment if convicted.

The genocide in Rwanda was sparked off by the assassination in April 1994 of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana. Angry Hutu mobs, militia and soldiers took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to Habyarimana's military junta. The mass slaughter ended after victorious Tutsi rebels took power and drove the Hutus into exile.
